_**Battletoads**_ is a 1991 [beat 'em up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_'em_up "Beat 'em up")platformvideo game developed by Rare and published by Tradewest for the Nintendo Entertainment System. The first installment of the _Battletoads_ series, it was released in North America and Japan in 1991 and in Europe in 1993. Ports without Rare's involvement were released on the Mega Drive and Game Gear in 1993, and on the Amiga and Amiga CD32 in 1994 (despite the former having been developed in 1992); a port developed by Rare for the Game Boy was released in 1993 as _**Battletoads in Ragnarok's World**_. In the game, three space humanoid warrior toads form a group known as the Battletoads. Two of the Battletoads, Rash and Zitz, embark on a mission to defeat the evil Dark Queen on her planet and rescue their kidnapped friends: Pimple, the third member of the Battletoads, and Princess Angelica.
The game was developed in response to the interest in Mirage Studios' _Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles_ franchise. It received mostly positive reviews upon release, with critics praising the graphics and variations of gameplay; however, many critics were divided over the game's difficulty. It won seven awards from the 1991 _Nintendo Power_ Awards, and has since been renowned as one of the most difficult video games ever created.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-7) It was later included in Rare's 2015 Xbox One retrospective compilation, _Rare Replay_, and was re-released on the Nintendo Classics service on November 26, 2025.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-11-26-2025-8)
The "Turbo Tunnel" level in the NES version

The game is a platformscrolling[beat 'em up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_'em_up "Beat 'em up"), with varying elements of racing, climbing and vehicle-based obstacle courses. Players start with three lives each time the game is started, which get replenished every time the player continues after getting defeated. The game contains no saving system or password features.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-retrospective-9) The player has a maximum of six hit points that can be replenished by eating flies.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTENES_instruction_manual199118-10) While the levels of _Battletoads_ vary greatly in gameplay style, the game is generally presented as a "[beat'em up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat'em_up "Beat'em up")", in which players progress by defeating enemies while avoiding the hazards in the environment.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-video-11)
Most of the attacks in the game have a "Smash Hit" variant, which triggers after a series of hits,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Nintendo_Power''_guide19919-12) or as the final hit to the enemy, and delivers a powerful blow to the enemy, often enlarging the body part delivering the blow.

The Toads's regular hit is a regular punch,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-GameZone-13) with its Smash Hit variant, "Kiss-My-Fist". Also, while running, which is done by tapping left or right on the D-pad twice in a row, the toads can deliver a head-butt.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTENES_instruction_manual19913-14) The head-butt's Smash Hit has the toads delivering a headbutt with giant ram horns, named the "Battletoad Butt". In addition, by standing close to them, most enemies can be picked up and thrown overhead.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-GameZone-13)

it involves the player going through the piping into the Gargantua, with sections including encounters with Mechno-Droids[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTENES_instruction_manual199112-18) and Steel-Beck duck creatures that guard the tubes,[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTENES_instruction_manual199111-48) chases from the Krazy Kog,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTENES_instruction_manual199112-18) and rivers infested with spikes, sharks, electric eels named Elctra-Eels, and instant-attacking Hammerfish.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTENES_instruction_manual199111-48)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Nintendo_Power''_guide199130%E2%80%9331-49)

The tenth level, Rat Race, is one of two levels in _Battletoads_ located in the Gargantua,[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Nintendo_Power''_guide199134-50) the other being the eleventh level, Clinger-Winger.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Nintendo_Power''_guide199136-39) Rat Race is a downward vertical-scrolling stage with the same hazards and enemies as Intruder Excluder.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Nintendo_Power''_guide199134%E2%80%9335-51) In the stage, the Dark Queen sends fast rodent Giblet to activate three bombs in the ship for it to explode, and the player must destroy the bombs before the rat makes it to them.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTENES_instruction_manual19918-29)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Nintendo_Power''_guide199134%E2%80%9335-51) After the bombs are successfully switched off, a showdown with the Queen's least quick-witted commander, General Slaughter who only attacks with his head, ensues.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Nintendo_Power''_guide199135-52)

The Battletoads escape the ship and, in another upward-vertical-scrolling stage named the Revolution, go to the top of the Dark Queen's Tower; the level involves the camera being fixed to the toads' position while the rest of the scenery rotates along with the circular tower as the toads go around it with a three-dimensional effect.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Nintendo_Power''_guide199138-53) In the level, a variety of platforms must be used as support in order to progress, including some that sink the longer the playable character is on them, those that disappear and re-appear, those that move around the tower, and springs; foes include oafs named Hornheads,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTENES_instruction_manual199114-33) Shadow Clouds that either harm the player with poisonous gas or blow wind to change the player's speed,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTENES_instruction_manual199116-38) Spiked Balls that rotate around the tower,[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTENES_instruction_manual199113-46) and Swellcheeks where player are required to hang from the flag poles to avoid being blown away by their wind power.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Nintendo_Power''_guide199138%E2%80%9339-20)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTENES_instruction_manual199114-33)

Once the toads reach the top of the tower, they will battle the Dark Queen. Once defeated, the Queen claims it will not be the last they would see from her. She then turns into a whirlwind and flies into space,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-54) "retreating into the shadowy margins of the galaxy to recoup her losses".[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-55) With Pimple and Princess Angelica rescued, the four are brought back into the _Vulture_ and fly away from the planet.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-56)

## Development and release
[edit]
> It was a typical example of Rare's looking at what was popular and then putting our spin on it.
The game was developed by Rare and published by Tradewest. Rare founders Tim and Chris Stamper created the series in response to the _Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles_ craze of the early 1990s.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-AllGame:_synopsis-57) To create a contrast to the popular media franchise and other beat 'em ups of the time, Rare added extra mechanics in the game to help separate it from these genres, such as racing stages and climbing courses.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-retrospective-9) Rare decided early to take the game's art style and tone in a cartoony direction, both to distance _Battletoads_ further from other beat 'em up franchises and to comply with Nintendo's restrictions on violence in games.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-BeforeYouDie-58):55

## Development and release
According to Rare artist Kevin Bayliss, the characters of _Battletoads_ were conceived in order to "produce merchandise" on a mass scale, in a similar vein to Tim Burton's _Batman_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-video-11) Bayliss claims that he did most of the work on sketching the game's characters while Tim Stamper was largely responsible for translating the sketches and artwork into sprites.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-BeforeYouDie-58):55 Rare attempted to create variation through shifts in gameplay between levels, and intentionally made _Battletoads_ "crazy hard" in order to increase its longevity. Bayliss frequently heard the team's programmer Mark Betteridge scream in anger after failing to complete levels he had assembled himself.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-BeforeYouDie-58):56 Despite their own difficulties, the team's consensus was that _Battletoads_ was possible to complete with practice and skill.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-BeforeYouDie-58):57
The game underwent changes through early stages of development, and at one point was originally titled _Amphibianz_. Bayliss originally designed _Battletoads_ as a Disney-themed video game, however as the game gradually became more violent, Bayliss took extra liberties to tone it down and restrict all usage of weapons in the game, whilst creating a sense of uniqueness for the characters.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-video-11) According to Bayliss, the box art was designed by him but airbrushed and produced by Tim Stamper. Bayliss' initial design for the box art was rejected as the team felt that it failed to attract customers' attention, but the team was satisfied with their second and final revision.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-BeforeYouDie-58):56–57

## Development and release
_Battletoads_ was presented at the Consumer Electronics Show in January 1991; an article about the event from _Electronic Gaming Monthly_ claimed it to be "highly innovative."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-59) A few months after the initial North American release in June 1991 for the NES, _Battletoads_ got a Japanese-localized release for the Famicom, getting distributed in Japan by NCS, as opposed to Tradewest.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-60) This release featured several gameplay tweaks, which resulted in a marginally easier experience.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-back-21)
By September 1992, the game had sold around 1.25 million NES cartridges in the United States.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-61)

## Development and release
_Battletoads_ was greeted with mostly enthusiastic reviews upon release, with critics calling it one of the best all-time video games,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-EGMNES-70) one of the best games of 1991,[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-GamePlay-89) one of the best all-time NES games,[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-mean-85)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-Dragon-67)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-CVG-22) and the greatest NES game of 1991.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-EGMNES-70) The "innovative and fun"[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-GPro-90) presentation was frequently praised,

The game is a platformscrolling[beat 'em up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_'em_up "Beat 'em up"), with varying elements of racing, climbing and vehicle-based obstacle courses. Players start with three lives each time the game is started, which get replenished every time the player continues after getting defeated. The game contains no saving system or password features.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-retrospective-9) The player has a maximum of six hit points that can be replenished by eating flies.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTENES_instruction_manual199118-10) While the levels of _Battletoads_ vary greatly in gameplay style, the game is generally presented as a "[beat'em up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat'em_up "Beat'em up")", in which players progress by defeating enemies while avoiding the hazards in the environment.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-video-11)
Most of the attacks in the game have a "Smash Hit" variant, which triggers after a series of hits,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Nintendo_Power''_guide19919-12) or as the final hit to the enemy, and delivers a powerful blow to the enemy, often enlarging the body part delivering the blow.
texts.4: The Toads's regular hit is a regular punch,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-GameZone-13) with its Smash Hit variant, "Kiss-My-Fist". Also, while running, which is done by tapping left or right on the D-pad twice in a row, the toads can deliver a head-butt.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTENES_instruction_manual19913-14) The head-butt's Smash Hit has the toads delivering a headbutt with giant ram horns, named the "Battletoad Butt". In addition, by standing close to them, most enemies can be picked up and thrown overhead.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-GameZone-13)

texts.14: The tenth level, Rat Race, is one of two levels in _Battletoads_ located in the Gargantua,[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Nintendo_Power''_guide199134-50) the other being the eleventh level, Clinger-Winger.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Nintendo_Power''_guide199136-39) Rat Race is a downward vertical-scrolling stage with the same hazards and enemies as Intruder Excluder.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Nintendo_Power''_guide199134%E2%80%9335-51) In the stage, the Dark Queen sends fast rodent Giblet to activate three bombs in the ship for it to explode, and the player must destroy the bombs before the rat makes it to them.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTENES_instruction_manual19918-29)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Nintendo_Power''_guide199134%E2%80%9335-51) After the bombs are successfully switched off, a showdown with the Queen's least quick-witted commander, General Slaughter who only attacks with his head, ensues.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Nintendo_Power''_guide199135-52)
texts.15: The Battletoads escape the ship and, in another upward-vertical-scrolling stage named the Revolution, go to the top of the Dark Queen's Tower; the level involves the camera being fixed to the toads' position while the rest of the scenery rotates along with the circular tower as the toads go around it with a three-dimensional effect.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Nintendo_Power''_guide199138-53) In the level, a variety of platforms must be used as support in order to progress, including some that sink the longer the playable character is on them, those that disappear and re-appear, those that move around the tower, and springs; foes include oafs named Hornheads,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTENES_instruction_manual199114-33) Shadow Clouds that either harm the player with poisonous gas or blow wind to change the player's speed,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTENES_instruction_manual199116-38) Spiked Balls that rotate around the tower,[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTENES_instruction_manual199113-46) and Swellcheeks where player are required to hang from the flag poles to avoid being blown away by their wind power.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''Nintendo_Power''_guide199138%E2%80%9339-20)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-FOOTNOTENES_instruction_manual199114-33)

She then turns into a whirlwind and flies into space,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-54) "retreating into the shadowy margins of the galaxy to recoup her losses".[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-55) With Pimple and Princess Angelica rescued, the four are brought back into the _Vulture_ and fly away from the planet.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-56)

## Development and release
[edit]
> It was a typical example of Rare's looking at what was popular and then putting our spin on it.
The game was developed by Rare and published by Tradewest. Rare founders Tim and Chris Stamper created the series in response to the _Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles_ craze of the early 1990s.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-AllGame:_synopsis-57) To create a contrast to the popular media franchise and other beat 'em ups of the time, Rare added extra mechanics in the game to help separate it from these genres, such as racing stages and climbing courses.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-retrospective-9) Rare decided early to take the game's art style and tone in a cartoony direction, both to distance _Battletoads_ further from other beat 'em up franchises and to comply with Nintendo's restrictions on violence in games.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-BeforeYouDie-58):55
texts.18:
## Development and release
According to Rare artist Kevin Bayliss, the characters of _Battletoads_ were conceived in order to "produce merchandise" on a mass scale, in a similar vein to Tim Burton's _Batman_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-video-11) Bayliss claims that he did most of the work on sketching the game's characters while Tim Stamper was largely responsible for translating the sketches and artwork into sprites.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-BeforeYouDie-58):55 Rare attempted to create variation through shifts in gameplay between levels, and intentionally made _Battletoads_ "crazy hard" in order to increase its longevity. Bayliss frequently heard the team's programmer Mark Betteridge scream in anger after failing to complete levels he had assembled himself.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-BeforeYouDie-58):56 Despite their own difficulties, the team's consensus was that _Battletoads_ was possible to complete with practice and skill.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-BeforeYouDie-58):57
The game underwent changes through early stages of development, and at one point was originally titled _Amphibianz_. Bayliss originally designed _Battletoads_ as a Disney-themed video game, however as the game gradually became more violent, Bayliss took extra liberties to tone it down and restrict all usage of weapons in the game, whilst creating a sense of uniqueness for the characters.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-video-11) According to Bayliss, the box art was designed by him but airbrushed and produced by Tim Stamper. Bayliss' initial design for the box art was rejected as the team felt that it failed to attract customers' attention, but the team was satisfied with their second and final revision.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-BeforeYouDie-58):56–57
texts.19:
## Development and release
_Battletoads_ was presented at the Consumer Electronics Show in January 1991; an article about the event from _Electronic Gaming Monthly_ claimed it to be "highly innovative."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-59) A few months after the initial North American release in June 1991 for the NES, _Battletoads_ got a Japanese-localized release for the Famicom, getting distributed in Japan by NCS, as opposed to Tradewest.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-60) This release featured several gameplay tweaks, which resulted in a marginally easier experience.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-back-21)
By September 1992, the game had sold around 1.25 million NES cartridges in the United States.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-61)
texts.20:
## Development and release
_Battletoads_ was greeted with mostly enthusiastic reviews upon release, with critics calling it one of the best all-time video games,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-EGMNES-70) one of the best games of 1991,[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-GamePlay-89) one of the best all-time NES games,[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-mean-85)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-Dragon-67)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-CVG-22) and the greatest NES game of 1991.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-EGMNES-70) The "innovative and fun"[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battletoads_(1991_video_game)#cite_note-GPro-90) presentation was frequently praised,

_**Adventure Fun-Pak**_ is a collection of four video games created by Scott Miller and various independent developers who submitted their programs to Apogee for publication. Miller categorized these submissions by genre and released this collection and the companion _Puzzle Fun-Pak_ as non-shareware commercial products. Each collection was sold as a single package distributed on one floppy disk.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-README-1) Apogee re-released both collections as freeware on 28 May 2004.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-ApogeePak-2) The following games are included:[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-GamePak-3)

*   _**Night Bomber**_ is an artillery game in which the player attempts to destroy as many cities as possible by issuing orders to a gun to fire projectiles at a specified angle.  
*   _**Raiders of the Forbidden Mine**_ (also known as _Raiders of the Lost Mine_, _Diamond Digger_ and _Gold Miner_) is a real-timeaction game with gameplay and a third-person perspective reminiscent of Dig Dug and Paganitzu. The objective is to collect as many gold nuggets as possible by maneuvering the player character through a series of levels situated in an underground mine while evading enemies capable of killing upon contact. Each level contains oxygen boxes to ensure the player character does not run out of breathable air and a key needed to unlock the door to the next level.  
*   _**Rogue Runner**_ (also known as _Maze Runner_) utilizes ASCII graphics to depict a maze from an overhead third-person perspective. Gameplay is similar to Apogee's _Kroz_ series; the objective in each level of the maze is to maneuver the player character in real-time through a series of corridors and evade enemies to find the entrance to the next level. Scattered throughout each level are pickaxes which may be used to kill attacking opponents, teleport scrolls capable of instantly transporting the player character to a random point within that level's maze, and maps which reveal the maze to the player in greater detail. The game ends when the player retrieves the Heart of Courage from the deepest level of the dungeon or is killed by contact with an enemy. Designed by Scott Miller, the game was also published under the name _Maze Runner_ in Softdisk's _Big Blue Disk_ #26 released in December 1988.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-BigBlueDisk-4)  
*   _**The Thing**_ is a port of _Hunt the Wumpus_ for MS-DOS.

_**Beyond the Titanic**_ is a text adventure game written by Scott Miller for MS-DOS in Pascal in September 1984.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-5) No images accompany the game's textual descriptions, but a variety of colors are employed to enhance the layout of the game's text. A panel near the top of the screen continuously displays the player's score and number of moves thus far. Also included is the ability to save the game and restore a previously saved game. The game begins on the sinking ship _Titanic_ from which an escape must be sought. Upon doing so the player character is swept away into a mysterious underground complex. The objective of the game is to escape these predicaments and find a way to return home to San Francisco.

Originally released in 1986 before Miller founded Apogee,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-ApogeeReleaseTimeline-6) the game was later branded and advertised[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-READALL-7) as an Apogee product. Both it and _Supernova_ are the only two games published by Apogee as traditional shareware.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-SupernovaFreeware1998-8) Miller permitted the full game to be freely copied and distributed by its users, but they were encouraged to "register" it by sending him a cash donation to compensate him for his effort, to "encourage the author to make new and better games" and to qualify for "telephone support and clues".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-9) Although he had hoped that donations accompanying user registrations would become a significant source of revenue, this expectation failed to be realized as most users did not register the game.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-MastersOfDoom-10) He concluded that this strategy was not the way to start.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-ApogeeReleaseTimeline-6) It seemed to him that gamers were "more apt to simply take what they could get for free"[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-MastersOfDoom-10) and that he needed to introduce a greater incentive to get users to register his games. Miller's experience with _Beyond the Titanic_ and _Supernova_ led him to develop the Apogee model which would become Apogee's standard method of marketing future releases.

_Beyond the Titanic_ was re-released as freeware by Apogee on March 10, 1998.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-11) The source code for the game was released as free software under the GPL-2.0-or-later license on March 20, 2009.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-OldGamesFreeware-12)

_**Jumpman Lives!**_ is an unauthorized 1991 MS-DOS remake of the _Jumpman_platform game released by Epyx in 1983. In _Jumpman_, the player character walks, jumps, and climbs ladders and ropes to clear each level of bombs. Both the original and the remake share the same plot: a multi-level orbital science station needs to be cleared of bombs planted by a radical group.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-Parker1991-13) In the original game the station orbits the planet Jupiter, but in the remake it is in orbit around Saturn.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-14) Included in the remake are levels from _Jumpman_, _Jumpman Junior_, and some newly created ones.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-SharplessInterview1-15) Other enhancements in the remake include a level editor, Sound Blaster support, and three skill levels.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-Matero-16)

Dave Sharpless designed and developed the game in cooperation with Apogee. Designed by Scott Miller, the game was also published in Softdisk's _Big Blue Disk_ #32 released in June 1989.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-BigBlueDisk-4)  
*   _**Maze Machine**_ generates an overhead map of a random maze with corridors of a height and width specified by the user. The program's output may be sent to a printer so that the maze can be solved by hand.  
*   _**Phrase Master**_ is a two playerturn-based game in which each player must guess which letters appear in a phrase the program randomly chooses from its stock of five hundred phrases. Each player continues to make guesses until he or she guesses incorrectly, at which point the other player's turn begins.
texts.10:
### Star Trek: The Next Generation Trivia
_**Supernova**_ is a text adventure video game designed by Scott Miller for MS-DOS and published by Apogee Software. The game's text was co-written by Scott Miller and Terry Nagy. Although _Supernova's_ plot is unrelated to that of Miller's previous text adventure _Beyond the Titanic_, its game engine and look and feel represent an evolutionary development from the earlier game. No images accompany the game's textual descriptions, but a variety of colors are employed to enhance the layout of the game's text. A panel near the top of the screen continuously displays the player's score, location, number of moves thus far, and the player character's condition (e.g. thirsty). Also included is the ability to save the game and restore a previously saved game. Miller wrote that the game features over four hundred sound effects, 16-color ASCII graphics, a hint command and a parser which recognizes over a thousand words.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-READALL-7) The game begins with the player character seeking employment on the surface of a barren mining planet. As the game progresses, the player discovers that an imminent supernova is threatening to destroy a planetary civilization. The main goal of the game is to save its inhabitants from this imminent catastrophe.
texts.11:
### Star Trek: The Next Generation Trivia
Originally released in 1987 before Miller founded Apogee,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-ApogeeReleaseTimeline-6) the game only made Miller around $1,000 while distributed through disk magazines like _I.B.Magazette_ and _Big Blue Disk_.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-SharewareHeroes-23) After the rights reverted to him, the game was later branded and advertised as an Apogee product.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-READALL-7) Both it and _Beyond the Titanic_ are the only two games published by Apogee as traditional shareware.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-SupernovaFreeware1998-8) Miller permitted the full game to be freely copied and distributed by its users, but they were encouraged to "register" it by sending him a cash donation to compensate him for his effort, to "encourage the author to make new and better games" and to qualify for "telephone support and clues".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-24) Although he had hoped that donations accompanying user registrations would become a significant source of revenue, this expectation failed to be realized as most users did not register the game.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-MastersOfDoom-10) He concluded that this strategy was not the way to start.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-ApogeeReleaseTimeline-6) It seemed to him that gamers were "more apt to simply take what they could get for free"[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-MastersOfDoom-10) and that he needed to introduce a greater incentive to get users to register his games.
texts.12:
### Star Trek: The Next Generation Trivia
Miller's experience with _Beyond the Titanic_ and _Supernova_ led him to develop the Apogee model which would become Apogee's standard method of marketing future releases.
Apogee also sold the game's Turbo Pascal 3.0 source code and marketed it to "novice programmers trying to learn the 'tricks of the trade'".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-READALL-7)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-25)
_Supernova_ was re-released as freeware by Apogee on March 26, 1998.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-SupernovaFreeware1998-8) The source code for the game was released as free software under the GPL-2.0-or-later license on March 20, 2009.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-OldGamesFreeware-12)

The game places the player trapped within the Caves of Thor. The object of the game is to locate three missing items scattered throughout the place. _**Trek Trivia**_ is a trivia video game about the _Star Trek_ TV series, written in Turbo Pascal 5.0 for MS-DOS and published by Apogee Software. The game consists of ten volumes each featuring 100 multiple choice questions related to _Star Trek_. Questions randomly chosen from the volume's database are sequentially presented to the player, who responds by selecting a numbered response from a list. For each correct answer, the game reveals a bonus _Star Trek_ fact. Players begin the game with three credits; every ten correct responses earn the player an additional credit, but each incorrect response costs the player one credit.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_minor_Apogee_Software_video_games#cite_note-26) When the player runs out of credits or has attempted all 100 questions, the game ends and the player's level of _Star Trek_ knowledge is ranked on the basis of how many questions were correctly answered. The earliest surviving version of Taipei is 1.02 from 3 April 1987 copyright Bogus Software. The source code for version 2.00 credits "David Norris and Hans Spiller" and jokes that "Bogus software does not do revision histories"4. Other versions included 3.10 (May 1990) and 3.50 (August 1990) with 3.50 adding a Help file and already requiring an ABOUTWEP.DLL file to run. However, it was version 4.00 that was released by Microsoft as part of WEP 1 while 5.00 was published by Norris in 1991 as shareware. These later versions credit Norris and thank Spiller "for ideas" except in the WEP version which does not mention Spiller.
Norris had written a chess game which he ported to Windows 3.0 on 11 October 1990 as "Win Chess 1.0"15. A second release of Win Chess 1.0 and a version 1.01 added more openings moves to its library and revamped Chess was released by Microsoft in WEP 4 (1992). The original version notes "This is the first released version of my WinChess chess program for Microsoft Windows". The Help file for version 2.0 explained that "As my Taipei program proved to be very popular as a shareware program, I've decided to make WinChess shareware as well" and he thanked "fellow bogusites" Hans and Ferg. The latter was Scott Ferguson who was hired in November 1986 and later became the Development Lead for Visual Basic.16,17 Ferguson wrote QUADominoes in July 1990 and it was released as TetraVex in WEP 3 (1991).
Win Chess 1.0 (1990) by Norris

Norris also released Mines 1.0 for Windows 3.0 sometime before June 1990 18. The objective was to find a path from the top left corner to the bottom right corner across a sea of mines using number clues. Although similar in some respects to Minesweeper a beta version of the latter noted "WinMine bears little resemblance to the other windows Mine game" and teases Norris that Taipei "was a blatant rip-off of a Macintosh game" called Shanghai (1986)18. Norris told this site he still had the source code and that his inspiration for the game probably "had something to do with wanting to write a path-finding algorithm"19.
Mines 1.0 (1990) by Norris
A famous Bogus Software program was the Fish! screensaver. During the summer of 1985 an artist in the tutorials team, Janet Vogelzang, asked Fries to convert her ASCII text pictures of fish into a screensaver. He made the MS-DOS screensaver in a few hours then asked for more fish and released an animated screensaver called "Microsoft Fish-O-Rama".8,9 When he returned in March 1986 he joined the Excel 2.0 team and ported the program to Windows as Microsoft Fish! 1.0 with a copyright date of 1987 9,12. In one version he says, "I made it so the spreadsheet could control a submarine in Fish, drive it around, shoot at the fish. It showed how live data could come in and out of Excel, and all the logic for controlling a submarine was recalculated in real-time in the spreadsheet."9
Fish! 1.0 (1987) by Fries

Excel 1.0 was only a Macintosh product so Fries decided to port his new screensaver to that platform 9. Saxton suggested creating a fish editor program and promptly wrote one himself 8,11. The pair released the screensaver and editor for both Macintosh and Windows in 1988 and Fries says, "We had put out a version that had an address on it for people to send the fish - just send fish - and instead of sending fish they started sending money."12 He continues, "We put the name Bogus Software on that, but we didn't want to just say 'Bogus Software,' since it was just Tom and me, so we called it Tom and Ed's Bogus Software."9 Fish! 3.0 was released in August 1991 with the Help file noting that "Tom & Ed's Bogus Software was founded in 1988 to accomplish a simple goal: to put 'A Fish on Every Desktop.' Win Fish brings our efforts to the world of Microsoft Windows 3.0."20
Spiller recalls, "One day, Ed Fries came to me wanting to take the name 'Bogus Software' to use for his shareware company for his fish program. This seemed kind of cool to me, as long as the real core of Bogus Software - the occasional recreational hack - would remain intact. So he and Tom Saxon called their company 'Tom and Ed's Bogus Software'."6 In the Help file for Space War! Spiller notes, "We have already granted Tom & Ed rights to the name, which is only right, since they are part of Bogus Software."14
Fish! 3.0 (1991) by Fries and Saxton

Dave Edson joined Microsoft in August 1988 to work on product support for the Windows SDK 21. He had already published several TRS-80 games such as Caterpillar (1982), Tube Frenzy (1982), Venturer (1982), Planet Raider (1982), Catch-Em (1982) and Tutankam (1983). The earliest surviving version of Taipei is 1.02 from 3 April 1987 copyright Bogus Software. The source code for version 2.00 credits "David Norris and Hans Spiller" and jokes that "Bogus software does not do revision histories"4. Other versions included 3.10 (May 1990) and 3.50 (August 1990) with 3.50 adding a Help file and already requiring an ABOUTWEP.DLL file to run. However, it was version 4.00 that was released by Microsoft as part of WEP 1 while 5.00 was published by Norris in 1991 as shareware. These later versions credit Norris and thank Spiller "for ideas" except in the WEP version which does not mention Spiller.
Norris had written a chess game which he ported to Windows 3.0 on 11 October 1990 as "Win Chess 1.0"15. A second release of Win Chess 1.0 and a version 1.01 added more openings moves to its library and revamped Chess was released by Microsoft in WEP 4 (1992). The original version notes "This is the first released version of my WinChess chess program for Microsoft Windows". The Help file for version 2.0 explained that "As my Taipei program proved to be very popular as a shareware program, I've decided to make WinChess shareware as well" and he thanked "fellow bogusites" Hans and Ferg. The latter was Scott Ferguson who was hired in November 1986 and later became the Development Lead for Visual Basic.16,17 Ferguson wrote QUADominoes in July 1990 and it was released as TetraVex in WEP 3 (1991).

texts.4:
Norris also released Mines 1.0 for Windows 3.0 sometime before June 1990 18. The objective was to find a path from the top left corner to the bottom right corner across a sea of mines using number clues. Although similar in some respects to Minesweeper a beta version of the latter noted "WinMine bears little resemblance to the other windows Mine game" and teases Norris that Taipei "was a blatant rip-off of a Macintosh game" called Shanghai (1986)18. Norris told this site he still had the source code and that his inspiration for the game probably "had something to do with wanting to write a path-finding algorithm"19.
Mines 1.0 (1990) by Norris
A famous Bogus Software program was the Fish! screensaver. During the summer of 1985 an artist in the tutorials team, Janet Vogelzang, asked Fries to convert her ASCII text pictures of fish into a screensaver. He made the MS-DOS screensaver in a few hours then asked for more fish and released an animated screensaver called "Microsoft Fish-O-Rama".8,9 When he returned in March 1986 he joined the Excel 2.0 team and ported the program to Windows as Microsoft Fish! 1.0 with a copyright date of 1987 9,12. In one version he says, "I made it so the spreadsheet could control a submarine in Fish, drive it around, shoot at the fish. It showed how live data could come in and out of Excel, and all the logic for controlling a submarine was recalculated in real-time in the spreadsheet."9

Excel 1.0 was only a Macintosh product so Fries decided to port his new screensaver to that platform 9. Saxton suggested creating a fish editor program and promptly wrote one himself 8,11. The pair released the screensaver and editor for both Macintosh and Windows in 1988 and Fries says, "We had put out a version that had an address on it for people to send the fish - just send fish - and instead of sending fish they started sending money."12 He continues, "We put the name Bogus Software on that, but we didn't want to just say 'Bogus Software,' since it was just Tom and me, so we called it Tom and Ed's Bogus Software."9 Fish! 3.0 was released in August 1991 with the Help file noting that "Tom & Ed's Bogus Software was founded in 1988 to accomplish a simple goal: to put 'A Fish on Every Desktop.' Win Fish brings our efforts to the world of Microsoft Windows 3.0."20
Spiller recalls, "One day, Ed Fries came to me wanting to take the name 'Bogus Software' to use for his shareware company for his fish program. # Helious
DOS- 1993
_Helious_ is a fun and unique arcade-style puzzler that is very hard to describe.
Essentially you must maneuver a balloon through 18 different worlds (9 in _Helious 1_, the shareware version, and the other 9 in _Helious 2_, the registered portion – both are included in the download here). In order to win the game, you must match up the icons by each colored ball with the icons found by completing each level. The trick in _Helious_ that makes the game challenging is that you must release a little air in the direction you want to move. Since air in a balloon is limited, you must conserve air as much as you can, and look out for air pump on each level that you an use to regain lost air. The balloon gets smaller and smaller as you lose air, until eventually it will pop, forcing you to restart the level. The levels are all filled with sharp, spiky objects and monsters, as well as other obstacles including locked doorways. Each level has a unique layout and graphics, which get weirder the more you play. The game basically requires you to squeeze through tight spots, search for air pumps and refills, capture keys to unlock doors, grab firepower, and even rain photon death upon vicious sharp objects.
Overall, _Helious_ is a fun game that requires patience and careful timing, as well sharp shooting skills. I was having fun for a while until the game’s very colorful and weird graphics became too frustrating for me, since I would have to spend a lot of time separating obstacles and monsters from the background graphics. If you can tolerate some eye strain, though, _Helious_ is an interesting game that is well worth a look, especially if you enjoy other “new age” style games such as _Vaxine_.
Note: formerly released as shareware with $9 cost of registration, _Helious_ is now freeware thanks to its designer, Sean Puckett.

## DOS games developed by Albino Frog Software
Albino Frog Software was the one-person studio of Sean M. Puckett, known earlier as Night Sky before adopting the Albino Frog name. From this small, inventive shop came a handful of distinctive DOS titles that earned a loyal following: the balloon-guiding action-puzzlers Helious and Helious II, the shooter Galacta: The Battle for Saturn, and the color-matching puzzler Pulse. The games were typically distributed as shareware, showcasing clever mechanics and quirky personality that stood out in the DOS era. You can play the studio’s confirmed DOS releases online for free and rediscover why these compact, creative projects still charm retro fans today.

# Helious
DOS- 1993
_Helious_ is a fun and unique arcade-style puzzler that is very hard to describe.
Essentially you must maneuver a balloon through 18 different worlds (9 in _Helious 1_, the shareware version, and the other 9 in _Helious 2_, the registered portion – both are included in the download here). In order to win the game, you must match up the icons by each colored ball with the icons found by completing each level. The trick in _Helious_ that makes the game challenging is that you must release a little air in the direction you want to move. Since air in a balloon is limited, you must conserve air as much as you can, and look out for air pump on each level that you an use to regain lost air. The balloon gets smaller and smaller as you lose air, until eventually it will pop, forcing you to restart the level. The levels are all filled with sharp, spiky objects and monsters, as well as other obstacles including locked doorways. Each level has a unique layout and graphics, which get weirder the more you play. The game basically requires you to squeeze through tight spots, search for air pumps and refills, capture keys to unlock doors, grab firepower, and even rain photon death upon vicious sharp objects.
Overall, _Helious_ is a fun game that requires patience and careful timing, as well sharp shooting skills. I was having fun for a while until the game’s very colorful and weird graphics became too frustrating for me, since I would have to spend a lot of time separating obstacles and monsters from the background graphics. If you can tolerate some eye strain, though, _Helious_ is an interesting game that is well worth a look, especially if you enjoy other “new age” style games such as _Vaxine_.
Note: formerly released as shareware with $9 cost of registration, _Helious_ is now freeware thanks to its designer, Sean Puckett.

## Description
Galacta: The Battle for Saturn is an action game that was published by Albino Frog Software Inc. It was released for DOS platforms in 1992 and is played from a top-down perspective.
The gameplay of the shooter game is similar to Galaga and Galaxian. Galacta: The Battle for Saturn provides you with a top-down space shooter similar to other arcade games.
In the game, the player moves frontwards and backward at the bottom of the screen to avoid attacks from the enemy ships. The player escapes the attacks from the enemies by moving on the screen and can even attack the enemy. When an enemy ship swoops at the player or the enemy attacks him, he dies. The enemies can attack the player in numerous pre-specified patterns. Staying out of the way of the enemies is the biggest challenge for the player.
The player needs to be careful when the ships fly down at him and they bounce back from the bottom of the screen and fly up again. The game features numerous powerups and shields to help him survive the attacks from the enemies. When the player manages the make it through the wave of enemies without getting killed, he receives a bonus to his score.
Galacta: The Battle for Saturn is a single-player game that can be played using an analog joystick. Shoot down all the enemies as you progress in the game while escaping the attacks. The goal is to get rid of all the enemies and succeed to the successive level.

## A vertical shooter paying homage to the great arcaders
It's not hard to see whom this game is referencing: It's got Galaxian written all over it, but, to its credit, the game doesn't just aim to recreate that experience, instead it aims to amend it, to explore it further and to see what other ideas can be executed on that particular frame of mind. Thus, Galacta - The Battle for Saturn, is a diverse game, a game that allows you to get a lot of fun, through the simple yet satisfying means of vertical space shooting; you control a ship that has to avoid projectiles, shoot down as many objects as possible and, generally, make sure to pick up all of the (desirable) upgrades. The game looks like a modern take on Galaxian, which is to say that while still 2D and pretty black infused, throughout, there are also visible upgrades to that oldschool era of gaming. Surely, it doesn't go full tilt kitsch, with loads of colors that will just mess with you, nope, it's pretty contained a game, but not a bad one, all things considered. So, yeah, go and take a look and see what it is all about. For vertical shooter fans, and for general purpose arcade lovers, it's a treat.

## 2D vertical arcade shooter, worth a shot!
Space Invaders invented the genre, Cheesy Invaders spoofed it and Galacta was just another game to try its hand at the recipe! Did it manage to bring in something at least a little original? Nope, I'm afraid not! But then again, what do we care if a game is original or not? It never said it would be, so the question should be, is it any fun? Well, in that respect, yes, Galacta holds its water. It gives you the basic enemies, the bosses and the swarms of enemies that require a certain type of combination of fire and movement to be eradicated (while you're safe from their firing patterns). Also, the game throws a number of power ups at you, power ups that improve your firepower in classic ways, by doubling your rate of fire, by doubling the number of weapons you have, by improving your speed of evasion and a few more. Manage to get shattered while carrying addons and you repeat the level, but without them. And that can be quite a bummer, especially during later levels when the action is hotter and the enemies more vicious. So, all things considered, Galacta is just another vertical shooter, but an okay one. Try it out, see if it clicks with or and if not, maybe the more colorful and diverse Raiden vertical shooter will hold the key to your heart.

Galacta - The Battle for Saturn is a vertical space shooter brought to us by Sean Puckett. Not to be confused with the Marvel character with the same name, the game while being considered decent, is not on par as many of the other games in the same genre, like with Invasion of the Mutant Space Bats of Doom.
